title: Tech Deep Dive: Multi-region Routing & Failover
summary: Deep technical discussion on multi-region routing, failover strategies, policy routing, regional capacity planning, DR playbooks. Covered routing policies (latency vs cost), model variant fallback, KV cache coherence across regions, batching/throughput tradeoffs, quantization impacts, and networking/VPC considerations for private deployments.
topics: KV cache strategy and cache warming
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-10
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Liam Zhou (Redwood), Jordan Lee (StratusHealth), Maya Patel (StratusHealth SRE), Samir Rao (StratusHealth Security), Elena Gomez (Product)

Auto-generated Summary: Technical deep dive on multi-region routing and failover for StratusHealth; focus on guaranteeing SLAs during regional outages and how Redwood routes, caches, and falls back to model variants and regions.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making the time. quick intros?
[00:06] Jordan: Jordan here, platform eng, I look after infra for our API layer.
[00:10] Maya: Maya, SRE, I'll be driving the DR requirements.
[00:14] Samir: Samir from security, I'll ask the compliance questions.
[00:17] Alex: great. Priya and Liam from our side will run through the design options.
[00:23] Priya: cool, our agenda, we'll go over routing policies, how Redwood determines region choice, capacity considerations, cache consistency for KV cache across regions, and then failure scenarios and playbooks. we'll also touch on batching and quantization tradeoffs for throughput.
[00:36] Liam: quick note, sorry, transcription might spell some things weird, like V P C or KV cahce, just ignore that.

[01:02] Priya: starting with policy routing - Redwood supports policy-based routing where requests are evaluated and routed by a policy engine. common policies: latency-first (route to nearest region), cost-first (route to cheaper region/low-cost tiers), capacity-aware (route where we have available reserved capacity), and compliance-based (route to regions with required data residency).
[01:25] Jordan: so for us, we need PII scope to stay within EU for EU patients, so compliance-based routing is critical. what happens on region failure - do you automatically send traffic to another EU region or to US fallback?
[01:38] Priya: by default policy respects data residency. you can set a failover policy: strict (no cross-region fallback, request fails), regional-fallback (try other EU region), global-fallback (go to any region, usually with redactions or with consent). most customers choose regional-fallback plus a manual escalation step for cross-region.
[02:02] Maya: we need RTO under 5 minutes for our API. can Redwood do that with cache warmup?
[02:10] Priya: depends. we have a few levers. prefix/KV cache can be replicated proactively between paired regions - we call this proactive cache warm. or we can do on-demand cache population which adds latency for first requests. proactive replication reduces RTO but costs more.
[02:27] Liam: for clarity, KV cache stores key-value token prefixes for large prompt reuse; in cross-region scenarios we either replicate the full cache snapshot or maintain a lightweight prefix index and fetch from origin. both have tradeoffs.
[02:41] Jordan: how big are these snapshots? our workload has lots of long-context prompts, could be big.
[02:46] Priya: they vary. typical active cache size per model can be tens to a few hundreds of MBs for heavy reuse, but for extreme workloads it can go into GBs. we recommend targeted replication for top N prefixes to keep warm.

[03:10] Maya: on autoscaling and regional capacity - you mentioned dedicated pools. how do you ensure we have capacity in region during a spike?
[03:20] Alex: Redwood Dedicated gives reserved capacity. you can provision baseline GPUs and configure burst policies to spill into adjacent regions or a shared burst pool. the autoscaler has hysteresis and lookahead policies to avoid thrash.
[03:33] Liam: capacity-aware routing will prefer regions with free slots for low-latency paths; if capacity is low, we'll consider routing to next-best region per policy. you can also configure hard pinning if you need strict locality.

[04:10] Samir: security: if we fall back cross-region, what about encryption and KMS? our KM S is in EU.
[04:17] Priya: for Private deployments we support integrated KMS/HSM and customer-managed keys. cross-region fallbacks require KMS access in the target region; we either replicate keys (if allowed) via your KMS replication or use proxying with strict audit logs. we'll provide an architecture doc.
[04:33] Samir: ok we'll need that. SOC 2 auditable trails for all cross-region data flows.

[05:00] Elena: can you walk through a DR playbook example? say eu-west-1 has a partial outage.
[05:08] Priya: sure. playbook example: 1) detect via health probes and metrics, 2) mark region degraded, shift routing to regional-fallback (eu-central), 3) pre-warm KV prefixes in eu-central (if proactive), 4) ramp traffic gradually with canary percentage, 5) monitor latency/quality and escalate to global-fallback only if allowed. each step has timeouts - detection (30-90s), warming (depends on prefix size, usually 1-5 minutes), canary ramp (couple minutes). total RTO target can be sub-5 minutes with proactive warm.
[05:50] Jordan: that warming time feels optimistic. if we have large KV caches won't it take longer?
[05:56] Priya: it can; that's why we suggest targeted replication for top user flows. also continuous background sync for hot prefixes keeps latency low.

[06:30] Maya: what about model variant fallback? e.g., we use a quantized 8-bit in eu-west to save cost - if we failover to a region that only has full fp16 model, will responses differ?
[06:42] Liam: yes, model variants can change output slightly. Redwood supports variant-aware routing: you can define compatibility tiers. in a failover we can fall back to functionally equivalent model variants, and we can flag responses as served by a fallback variant so your app can decide to re-run or degrade gracefully.
[07:00] Priya: also, we do quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets, so you'll be alerted if the fallback model causes regressions.

[07:30] Jordan: latency numbers - what's expected added latency for cross-region? if we route EU->US fallback network latency alone could be 120-200ms, plus model inference.
[07:40] Liam: correct. network RTT plus inference differences. that's why policy routing usually prioritizes latency-first for user-facing flows. for background jobs you can pick cost-first and get higher tail latency.

[08:10] Samir: VPC networking for Private - do you support VPC peering across regions or require a transit gateway?
[08:16] Priya: we support customer-managed networking. options: VPC peering within same cloud, transit gateway for multi-region, or a private VPN/MPLS to your datacenter. specifics depend on your cloud provider. we will provide network diagrams.

[09:00] Jordan: a question on batching - if we start routing requests across regions, does batching get less efficient and hurt throughput?
[09:10] Liam: yes, batching efficiency depends on co-location of requests. global distribution reduces cross-request batching opportunities. Redwood's runtime uses continuous batching within each region; when traffic is sharded, each region batches independently. to mitigate you can route non-latency critical traffic to a centralized region to maximize batching.
[09:34] Priya: also, we support adaptive batching parameters so you can tune max batch size and timeout to balance latency vs throughput per region.

[10:00] Maya: any guidance on quantization when planning multi-region? are quantized models portable across regions/hardware?
[10:07] Liam: quantization compatibility depends on hardware and runtime. we provide quantized artifacts for supported hardware targets. if a target region lacks the optimized kernel for a specific quantized format, we may fall back to a different quantized variant or to fp16. that can slightly change performance and quality. we recommend validating prompt sets against each variant during onboarding.

[10:40] Jordan: what about cache coherence - if a user has session state in KV cache in eu-west and fails over to eu-central, is session state lost?
[10:48] Priya: by default session-local KV cache is region-scoped. you have options: replicate session state synchronously (costly), or persist session state to your backend and attach on failover, or do asynchronous replication for hot sessions. many customers persist critical session state in their own store (e.g., Redis with cross-region replication) and keep Redwood's KV as a short-lived accelerator.

[11:20] Samir: for compliance we prefer no cross-region replication of PII. so we'd do session persistence in our EU-only Redis that replicates to other EU regions.
[11:28] Priya: that aligns with the compliance-first routing policy.

[11:40] Alex: let's go through a couple of failure scenarios quick - total region outage, partial GPU failures, and network partition.
[11:46] Priya: total region outage: detection -> mark degraded -> regional-fallback -> canary -> full shift. partial GPU failures: autoscaler replaces capacity if you have Dedicated; workload shifts to instances with lower load. network partition (control-plane unreachable): runtime has local health checks and can operate in degraded mode serving cached requests and buffering metrics, and control plane reconciliation happens later.

[12:30] Jordan: reconcile timelines - how long until the control-plane catch-up?
[12:34] Liam: depends on the window length; we queue events and reconcile in minutes. critical routing decisions are made locally by the edge router so traffic keeps flowing per last-known policies.

[13:00] Maya: show of hands, how do you test these failovers? can Redwood run DR drills with us?
[13:06] Priya: yes, we run canary failover exercises with customers. we can simulate region outage in a staging environment or run partial traffic shift. we'll coordinate the blast radius and rollback steps.

[13:30] Elena: what's the monitoring surface we get? dashboards, per-route metrics?
[13:34] Alex: Redwood Console exposes per-model and per-route latency, token cost, error rates, and KV hit rates. for DR we'll share a runbook with alert thresholds and recommended SLOs.

[14:10] Jordan: cost implications - proactive cache replication and reserved capacity sounds expensive. any ballpark?
[14:17] Liam: proactive replication cost is mainly network and storage; reserved Dedicated GPUs are a fixed monthly cost. ballpark: proactive replication for top prefixes might be low hundreds per month, dedicated capacity in region is thousands to tens of thousands depending on size. we'll provide a sizing and cost estimate after we see your telemetry.

[15:00] Samir: action items around security docs and architecture.

[15:10] Priya: quick note on tooling: you can set routing policies via API or Console, and we support per-route overrides and emergency kill-switch.

[15:30] Jordan: a specific question - can we pin a model version to region A but allow read-only traffic from region B?
[15:38] Priya: yes, you can pin and then set a read-fallback that proxies requests to the pinned region while marking latency. it's essentially proxy-mode.

[16:00] Maya: latency SLO tracking - if we failover, can you annotate trace spans to show fallback path for our SLO dashboard?
[16:07] Liam: yes, we attach routing metadata to traces and provide trace tags for fallback-region, model-variant, and cache-hit. you can export to your tracing backend.

[16:30] Jordan: any pitfalls you've seen in production customers?
[16:35] Priya: common pitfalls: over-reliance on large global KV caches without a warming strategy, not validating model variants across regions, and insufficient alerting thresholds causing noisy failovers. also misconfigured network egress/KMS leading to unexpected auth failures during failover.

[17:00] Samir: about logs and audits - do you provide the full audit trail for cross-region access?
[17:06] Alex: yes, audit logs include routing decisions, model variant IDs, KMS operations, and user request IDs. we can extend retention as an add-on.

[17:30] Priya: let's propose a recommended blueprint for StratusHealth: 1) Define compliance-first routing policy (EU data residency), 2) Provision Dedicated baseline in primary EU region + smaller Dedicated in secondary EU region for capacity, 3) Enable targeted KV prefix replication for top flows, 4) Run failover DR drill with warm-up, 5) Instrument quality checks and regression alerts for model variants.
[18:05] Jordan: sounds good. can you share a templated playbook?
[18:09] Priya: yes, we'll send a playbook and topology diagrams.

[18:30] Elena: what about timeline - we want a pilot in 4 weeks. feasible?
[18:36] Alex: yes, pilot in 4 weeks reasonable: week 1 onboarding and network setup, week 2 model and cache tuning, week 3 DR drill, week 4 pilot ramp.

[19:00] Liam: I'll call out a few gotchas in the doc: ensure KMS replication permissions are in place, pick top-500 prefixes for warm, and set batch timeouts per route.

[19:30] Alex: ok let's go to open Q/A -
[19:36] Jordan: small nit - what's the behavior of streaming when failing over mid-stream? do you cut the connection?
[19:42] Priya: streaming is connection-bound; if we failover mid-stream, we attempt client resume where possible, but often the client must re-open the stream and we'll continue from the last token in KV if available. we recommend short-lived streams for critical paths or sticky routing for sessions.

[20:10] Maya: SLA question - do you offer SLA credits for cross-region outage?
[20:16] Alex: SLA covers infrastructure uptime and is tied to Dedicated and Private contracts. cross-region failovers are part of normal operations; credits apply if Redwood does not meet SLA for the committed region.

[20:40] Samir: can we get encryption in transit logs for cross-region egress?
[20:44] Priya: yes, TLS + mTLS for inter-region traffic and we log flow metadata. we can show sample logs.

[21:10] Jordan: how do we control rollbacks if a fallback model introduces regression?
[21:16] Liam: we have automatic rollback triggers based on quality monitors. you can opt-in to automatic rollback or manual. plus you can set per-prompt evaluation thresholds.

[21:40] Elena: we want to keep user experience seamless; are there UX flags we should use to degrade gracefully?
[21:47] Priya: include fallback metadata in responses (header or structured field) so the app can show a subtle note or hide features. we also recommend A/B style routing to compare fallbacks.

[22:10] Alex: approaching the last 20 minutes - going to summarize next steps and action items.
[22:16] Priya: recap: send security & architecture docs, send DR playbook, provide cost/size estimate, schedule DR drill, configure initial routing policy in staging.

[22:40] Jordan: one more thing - do you have an example of routing policy JSON?
[22:44] Liam: yes, we'll include policy snippets and Console screenshots.

[23:00] Samir: any competitor gaps we should be aware of?
[23:04] Alex: competitors often lack integrated KV replication, or they force customers to build their own model-variant monitoring. Redwood's edge is built-in instrumentation and runbooks.

[23:30] Maya: thanks all, that was helpful.

[23:36] Jordan: thanks, talk soon.

[23:50] Alex: we'll follow up by EOD with docs and proposed timelines.

End of transcript.
